meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'рогой'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('expensive; dear').

examples.text: В Москве вам дают деньги на дорогую одежду, а мозги не дают.
examples.trans: In Moscow they give you money for expensive clothes, but they don't give you brains.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'friend' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is Vanya, my childhood friend.

examples.text: Это Паша, мой заместитель. Это Ваня, друг моего детства.
examples.trans: This is Pasha, my deputy. This is Vanya, my childhood friend.

проходить.gloss: to go through; to come in

meanings.en: to go through; to come in
meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'ходить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to go through; to come in', paired with 'пройти'.

examples.text: Вика, Паша! Как я рад. Проходите, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: Vika, Pasha! I'm so glad. Come in, please.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for; behind', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'толик'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'small table, café table' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Они заняли свободный столик у окна.
examples.trans: They took a free table near the window.
Would you like to sit at an available table?
To a guest at the next table.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes, indeed', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'частье'). Common neuter noun meaning 'happiness' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: How much money is needed for happiness?

examples.text: Сколько миллионов нужно человеку для счастья?
examples.trans: How many millions does a person need for happiness?

meanings.note: Abstract feminine noun formed with the Slavic suffix '-ость' ('-ness, -ity') from the corresponding adjective. Common feminine noun meaning 'nonsense, foolishness' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Что за глупости? Значит, Осипенко сам эти деньги украл!
examples.trans: What nonsense? That means Osipenko stole that money himself!

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'health' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Конфликты с соседями угрожают здоровью подсудимого.
examples.trans: Conflicts with the neighbours threaten the defendant's health.

следить.gloss: to watch, to follow; to keep an eye on

meanings.en: to watch, to follow; to keep an eye on
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ледить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to watch, to follow; to keep an eye on', paired with 'проследить'.

examples.trans: Keep an eye on the child.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'this', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'частливчик'). Derived noun with agent/object suffix '-ник'/'-щик'/'-чик'. Common masculine noun meaning 'lucky guy' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Vika, keep a close eye on that lucky fellow.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новый счастливчик.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new lucky guy.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'to, towards', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'end' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: At the end of the film everyone is happy.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'вадьба'). Common feminine noun meaning 'wedding' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Watch the movie Wedding on Skype.

examples.text: Макс, зачем ты соврал про нашу будущую свадьбу?
examples.trans: Max, why did you lie about our future wedding?
Then a wedding, and then kids!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'along; by; about', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Это Аракелян. Я по поводу торгового центра.
examples.trans: It's Arakelyan. I'm calling about the shopping centre.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'peace; world' in everyday Russian.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

пустить.gloss: to let go; to let in

meanings.en: to let go; to let in
meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to let go; to let in', paired with 'пускать'.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'such, like this', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('good, nice').

examples.text: Какое хорошее утро! Лидия Алексеевна, чашку кофе, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: What a lovely morning! Lidia Alekseyevna, a cup of coffee, please.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'везти'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'got lucky', paired with 'везти'.

examples.trans: A lucky break: Tretyakov called back.
Soon this chronicle will be taken back.

examples.text: Мне обязательно сегодня должно повезти здесь.
examples.trans: I definitely must get lucky here today.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?
